questions.q: In a class of $140$ students numbered $1$ to$140$ , all even numbered students opted Mathematics course, those whose number is divisible by $3$ opted Physics course and those whose number is divisible by $5$ opted Chemistry course. Then the number of students who did not opt for any of the three courses is:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$From the given& $140$~students, all even numbered students opted Mathematics~\left(M\right),$~hence, the number of students opted Mathematics is~$M ≡ \left[\dfrac{140}{2}\right] =70,$~where~\left[x\right]$~denotes the greatest integer function of~$x .$

Similarly, the students who opted Physics are~$P ≡ \$left[\dfrac{140}{3}\right] =$46$

And, the~students who opted Chemistry are~$C ≡ \left[\dfrac{140}{5}\right] =28$

Similarly, the students who opted Mathematics and~Physics are the numbers which are divisible by both~$2 \text{ and } 3$~i.e.~$6,$~and their number is~$\$left[\dfrac{140}{6}\right] =$23$

The students who opted Mathematics and~Chemistry are the numbers which are divisible by both~$2 \text{ and } 5$~i.e.~$10,$~and their number is~\left[\dfrac{140}{10}\right] =14$

The students who opted Physics and~Chemistry are the numbers which are divisible by both~$3 \text{ and } 5$~i.e.~$15,$~and their number is~$\$left[\dfrac{140}{15}\right] =$9$

And, the students who opted all the three subjects are the numbers which are divisible by~$2, 3 \text{ and } 5$~i.e.~$30,$~and their number is~\left[\dfrac{140}{30}\right] =4$

Now, using
$n\left(P ∪ C ∪ M\right) = n\left(P\right) + n\left(C\right) + n \left($M\right) - n \left(P ∩ C\right) - n \left($C ∩ M\right) - $n\left($M ∩ P\right) + $n\left($P ∩ M ∩ C\right)$

$= 46 + 28 + 70 - 9 - 14 - 23 + 4$

$= 102$

Thus,~$102$~students have opted for atleast one of the three subjects.

Hence, number of students who did not opt for any of the three courses $= 140 - 102 = 38 .$

$

questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{A}: \log _{2 \pi}|\sin \mathrm{x}|+\log _{2 \pi}|\cos \mathrm{x}|=2 \\ & \Rightarrow \log _{2 \pi}(|\sin \mathrm{x} \cdot \cos \mathrm{x}|)=2 \\ & \Rightarrow|\sin 2 \mathrm{x}|=\frac{8}{\pi^2}\end{aligned}$
Number of solution 4 $\text { B : let } \sqrt{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{t} \lt 2$ Then $\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-4)+3(\sqrt{x}-2)+6=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}^2-4 \mathrm{t}+3 \mathrm{t}-6+6=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}^2-\mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{t}=0, \mathrm{t}=1 \\ & \mathrm{x}=0, \mathrm{x}=1 \end{aligned}$ again let $\sqrt{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{t} \gt 2$ then $\mathrm{t}^2-4 \mathrm{t}-3 \mathrm{t}+6+6=0\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}^2-7 \mathrm{t}+12=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{t}=3,4 \\ & \mathrm{x}=9,16 \end{aligned}$ Total number of solutions $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{~A} \cup \mathrm{~B})=4+4=8$

questions.q: If $R$ is the smallest equivalence relation on the set ${ 1, 2, 3, 4 }$ such that ${ ( 1, 2 ) , ( 1, 3 ) } ⊂ R$, then the number of elements in $R$ is ______.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given: $R = \left\{\left(1, 3\right), \left(1, 2\right)\right\}$

To make $R$ as Reflexive, the required elements are \left(1, 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left($3, 3\right)\text{and}\left(4, 4\right)$

To make $R$ as Symmetric, the required elements are \left(3, 1\$right)\text{and}\left($2, 1\right)$

To make $R$ as Transitive, the required elements are \left(3, 2\$right)\text{and}\left($2, 3\right)$

So, $8$ elements are required to make $R$ an equivalence relation.

Hence, the total number of elements in $R$ is $10.

$

questions.q: Let $A = \left\{1, 3, 4, 6, 9\right\}$ and $B = \left\{2, 4, 5, 8, 10\right\}$. Let $R$ be a relation defined on $A \times B$ such that $R = \left\{\left({a}_{1}, \left{b}_{1}\right), \left({a}_{2}, {b}_{2}\right): {a}_{1} \le {b}_{2}\right\text{and}{b}_{1} \le {a}_{2}\right\}$. Then the number of elements in the set $R$ is
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$A = \left\{1, 3, 4, 6, 9\right\} \text{ and } B = \left\{2, 4, 5, 8, 10\right\}$

And relation is given by,

$R = \left\{\left({a}_{1}, \left{b}_{1}\right), \left({a}_{2}, {b}_{2}\right): {a}_{1} \le {b}_{2}\right\text{and}{b}_{1} \le {a}_{2}\right\}$

Now taking cases for~${a}_{1} \le {b}_{2}$~we get,

${a}_{1} = 1, {b}_{2} \in \left\{2, 4, 5, 8, 10\right\} \to 5\text{cases}$

${a}_{1} = 3, {b}_{2} \in \left\{4, 5, 8, 10\right\} \to 4\text{cases}$

${a}_{1} = 4, {b}_{2} \in \left\{4, 5, 8, 10\right\} \to 4\text{cases}$

${a}_{1} = 6, {b}_{2} \in \left\{8, 10\right\} \to 2\text{cases}$

${a}_{1} = 9, {b}_{2} \in \left\{10\right\} \to 1\text{cases}$

So, total~$16$~cases will be there~

Now finding cases of~${b}_{1} \le {a}_{2}$~we get,

${b}_{1} = 2, {a}_{2} \in \left\{3, 4, 6, 9\right\} \to 4\text{cases}$

${b}_{1} = 4, {a}_{2} \in \left\{4, 6, 9\right\} \to 3\text{cases}$

${b}_{1} = 5, {a}_{2} \in \left\{6, 9\right\} \to 2\text{cases}$

${b}_{1} = 8, {a}_{2} \in \left\{9\right\} \to 1\text{cases}$

So, here total~$10$~cases,

Hence, total elements in relation~$= 16 \times 10 = 160$

questions.q: Consider the relations ${R}_{1}$ and ${R}_{2}$ defined as $a{R}_{1}b ⇔ a^{2} + b^{2} = 1$ for all $a, b, \in R$ and \left(a, b\right){R}_{2}\left(c, d\right) ⇔ a + d = b + c$ for all \left(a, b\right), \left(c, d\right) \in N \times N$. Then
options: Neither ${R}_{1}$ nor ${R}_{2}$ is an equivalence relation
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$a{R}_{1}b ⇔ a^{2} + b^{2} = 1; a, b \in R$

${R}_{1}$ is not reflexive as \left(a, a\right) \notin a{R}_{1}b$

So, it is not equivalence.

Now, solving

\left(a, b\right){R}_{2}\left(c, d\right) ⇔ a + d = b + c; \left(a, b\right), \left(c, d\right) \in N$

Reflexive: $a + b = b + a \to True$

Symmetric: \left(a, b\right){R}_{2} \left(c, d\right)$

$⇒ a + d = b + c$

$⇒ d + a = c + b$

$⇒ c + b = d + a$

$⇒ \left(c, d\right){R}_{2} \left(a, b\right)$

Transitive: \left($a, b\right){R}_{2} \left(c, d\right) ⇒ a + d = b + c . . . \left(i\right)$

\left($c, d\right){R}_{2} \left($e, f\right) ⇒ c + f = d + e . . . \left($ii\right)$

Now, adding above equation we get,

$⇒ a + f = b + e$

$⇒ \left(a, b\right){R}_{2} \left(e, f\right)$

So, ${R}_{2}$ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive

Hence only ${R}_{2}$ is equivalence relation.

$

questions.q: Let $Z$ be the set of integers. If $A = \left\{x \in Z: {2}^{\left(x + 2\right)\left(x^{2} - 5x + 6\right)} = 1\right\}$ and $B = { x \in Z: - 3 < 2x - 1 < 9 }$, then the number of subsets of the set $A \times B$, is :
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given ${2}^{\left(x + 2\right)\left(x - 2\right)\left(x - 3\right)} = 1 = {2}^{0} ⇒ x = - 2, 2, 3$.

$∴ n\left(A\right) = 3$

Again, $- 3 < 2x - 1 < 9 ⇒ - 1 < x < 5$

$⇒ x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$

$∴ n\left(B\right) = 5$

$∴ n\left(A \times B\right) = 3 \times 5 = 15$

$∴$Number of subset of $A \times B = {2}^{15}$

questions.q: A survey shows that& $63 %$ of the people in a city read newspaper $A$ whereas~$76 %$ read news paper $B$. If~ $x %$~of the people read both the newspapers, then a possible value of~$x$ can be:
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
$n\left(A\right) = 63$

$n\left(B\right) = 76$

$n\left(A ∩ B\right) = x$

Let~$n\left(∪\right) = 100$

$n\left(A ∪ B\right) = n\left(A\right) + n\left(B\right) - n\left(A ∩ B\right) \le 100$

$⇒ 63 + 76 - x \le 100$

$⇒ x \ge 39$

But~$n \left(A ∩ B\right) ≤ n \left($A\right)$

$∴ 39 ≤ x ≤ 63$& .

$

questions.q: For $\alpha \in N$, consider a relation $R$ on $N$ given by $R =${\left(x, y\right): 3x + \alphay$ is a multiple of $7}. The relation $R$ \text{ and } is an equivalence relation if and only if
options: $4$is the remainder when $\alpha$ is divided by~$10$
$4$~is the remainder when $\alpha$ is divided by~$7$
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given, a relation $R$ on $N$ given by $R =${\left(x, y\right): 3x + \alphay$ is a multiple of $7},

Now for $R$~to be reflexive~$⇒ xRx$

$⇒ 3x + \alphax = 7x$

$⇒ \left(3 + \alpha\right)x = 7K$

$⇒ 3 + \alpha = 7\lambda$

$⇒ \alpha = 7\lambda - 3 = 7N + 4, \left\{\text{where}K, \lambda, N \in I\right\}$

So, when $\alpha$ divided by $7$, remainder is $4$.

Now~$R$~to be symmetric~$xRy ⇒ yRx$

$3x + \alphay = 7{N}_{1}, 3y + \alphax = 7{N}_{2}$

$⇒ \left(3 + \alpha\right)\left(x + y\right) = 7\left({N}_{1} + {N}_{2}\right) = 7{N}_{3}$

Which holds when $3 + \alpha$ is multiple of~$7$

So,~$\alpha = 7N + 4$~(as did earlier)

Now, for~$R$~to be transitive

$xRy \text{ and } yRz ⇒ xRz .$

$⇒ 3x + \alphay = 7{N}_{1} . . . . \left(1\right)$

$⇒ 3y + \alphaz = 7{N}_{2} . . . . . . \left(2\right)$

And $3x + \alphaz = 7{N}_{3} . . . . . \left(3\right)$

Now subtracting equation~ \left($3\right) - \left(2\right)$~we get,~

$3x + 7{N}_{2} - 3y = 7{N}_{3}$

Now putting the value of~$3x$~from equation~ \left($1\right)$~we get,~$7{N}_{1} - \alphay + 7{N}_{2} - 3y = 7{N}_{3}$

$⇒ $7\left({N}_{1} + {N}_{2}\right) - \left(3 + \alpha\right)y = 7{N}_{3}$

$⇒ \left(3 + \alpha\right)y = 7N$

Which is true again when $3 + \alpha$divisible by $7$, i.e. when $\alpha$divided by $7$, remainder is~$4$ .

$

questions.q: An organization awarded $48$ medals in event $A ' '$, $25$ in event $B ' '$ and $18$ in event $C ' '$. If these medals went to total $60$ men and only five men got medals in all the three events, then, how many received medals in exactly two of three events?
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Let $A, B$ and $C$ denote the set of men who received medals in even $A$, event $B$~and event~$C$~respectively.

Then,~$n\left(A\right) = 48, n\left(B\right) = 25, n\left(C\right) = 18$~,~$n\left(A ∪ B ∪ C\right) = 60$~and $n\left(A ∩ B ∩ C\right) = 5$,

Now we know that,~$n\left(A ∪ B ∪ C\right) = n\left(A\right) + n\left(B\right) + n \left(C\right) - n \left(A ∩ B\right) - n \left(A ∩ C\right) - n\left(B ∩ C\right) + n\left(A ∩ B ∩ C\right)$

$⇒ 60 = 48 + 25 + 18 - n ( A ∩ B ) - n ( A ∩ C ) - n ( B ∩ C ) + 5$

$⇒ n ( A ∩ B ) + n ( A ∩ C ) + n ( A ∩ C ) = 48 + 25 + 18 + 5 - 60 = 36$

Therefore, the number of people who received medals in exactly two of the three sports will be~$36 - 3\left(A ∩ B ∩ C\right) = 36 - 15 = 21.

$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

In a group of& $100$~persons~$75$~speak English and~$40$~speak Hindi,~

And each person speaks at least one of the two languages,

And the number of persons who speak only English is~$\alpha$~and the number of persons who speaks only Hindi is~$\beta$,

Now from above diagram we can see that,

$\beta = 100 - 75 = 25$

So,~$\alpha = 75 - \left(40 - 25\right) = 60$

Hence, number of people who speak English only is~$\alpha = 60$~and Hindi is~$\beta = 25$,

Now putting the value in given equation of ellipse we get,

$25\left[\dfrac{x2}{602} + \dfrac{y2}{252}\right] = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{x2}{36 \times 4} + \dfrac{y2}{25} = 1$

Now comparing with~$\dfrac{x2}{a2} + \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1$~we get,~$a = 12 \text{ and } b = 5$

Now we know that,~

Eccentricity of ellipse is given by~$e = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{b2}{a2}}$

$⇒ e = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{25}{36 \times 4}} = \dfrac{119}{12}$

questions.q: Let $A = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}$ and $R = \left\{( 1, 2 ) , ( 2, 3 ) , ( 1, 4 )\right\}$ be a relation on $A$. Let $S$ be the equivalence relation on $A$ such that $R ⊂ S$ and the number of elements in $S$ is $n$. Then, the minimum value of $n$ is _______
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

$A = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}$ and $R = \left\{( 1, 2 ) , ( 2, 3 ) , ( 1, 4 )\right\}$ be a relation on $A$.

Now, given $S$ be the equivalence relation on $A$ and $R ⊂ S$

So, for $S$ to be equivalence it should be Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive on given relation,

Now, for reflexive Relation we need, \left\{\left(1, 1\right), \left(2, 2\right), \left(3, 3\right), \left(4, 4\right)\right\} \to 4$ elements,

For Symmetric relation we need, \left\{\left(2, 1\right), \left(3, 2\right), \left(4, 1\right)\right\} \to 3$ elements,

And for Transitive relation we need, \left\{\left(1, 3\right), \left(3, 1\right), \left(3, 4\right), \left(4, 2\right), \left(2, 4\right), \left(4, 3\right)\right\} \to 6$ elements

So, minimum $13$ elements should be added in $R$

Hence , $n\left(S\right) = 16$ elements.

$

questions.q: Let $A = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}$ and $R$ be a relation on the set $A \times A$~defined by $R = \left\{\left(\left(a, b\right), \left(c, d\right)\right): 2a + 3b = 4c + 5d\right\}$. Then the number of elements in $R$ is _________.
questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.solution:
Given,

Set& $A = \left\{1, 2, 3, 4\right\}$

And relation on $A \times A$~as~$2a + 3b = 4c + 5d$

Now, Maximum value of~$2a + 3b = 20$~at~ \left(4, 4\right)$

And Minimum value of~$4c + 5d = 9$~at~ \left(1, 1\right)$

So,~$4c + 5d$~can be equal to~$9, 13, 14, 17, 18, 19$

Now~$2a + 3b$~can be~$9$~if \left(a, b\right) = \left(3, 1\right) ⇒ \left($c, d\right) = \left($1, 1\right)$

Similarly,~$2a + 3b$~can be~$13$, if~ \left(a, b\right) = \left(2, 3\right) ⇒ \left($c, d\right) = \left($2, 1\right)$

And~$2a + 3b$~can be~$14$, if~ \left($a, b\right) = \left($4, 2\right)\text{or}\left($1, 4\right)$

$⇒ \left($c, d\right) = \left(1, 2\right)$

Similarly,~$2a + 3b$~can be~$17$, if~ \left($a, b\right) = \left(4, 3\right) ⇒$~\left(c, d\right) = \left(3, 1\right)$

And~$2a + 3b$~can be~$18$~if~\left(a, b\right) = \left(3, 4\right) ⇒$

\left(c, d\right) = \left(2, 2\right)$

Hence, there are total~$6$& elements which satisfy the given relation.
